He noted that it extends beyond media to the very heart of diplomacy, adding that those who own the signal shape the future, tell their story with authenticity, and earn the world's trust and respect. "The UAE does not seek the signalâit creates it," he stated.

Recent findings suggest that his Excellency explained that the global media landscape is changing at an unprecedented pace, with digital platforms shaping public awareness and attitudes. He added that owning media platforms is no longer sufficient, and reach alone is no measure of influence. Those who own the signal today, he remarked, are those who understand change, know their audiences, and present a comprehensive national narrative with a clear vision and message.

It has been revealed that H.E. Alshamsi emphasized the importance of communication tools in modern diplomacy, explaining that building trust now extends beyond dialogue forums and bilateral meetings to encompass media engagement. Audiences, he noted, look beyond official statements to images, stories, and positions.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that at age 23, Phil Shawe was pursuing an MBA at NYU when he had a business idea that made some people around him skeptical.
  • It has been revealed that shawe saw an opening.
  • “I met my former partner in business school, and she had worked at the largest translation company at the time, Berlitz,” Shawe indicates in a new interview with Entrepreneur.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that at age 23, Phil Shawe was pursuing an MBA at NYU when he had a business idea that made some people around him skeptical. Why spend money on business school, thousands of dollars, only to start a small translation company?

It has been revealed that shawe saw an opening. Advertising agencies, law firms and big corporations needed language services. He believed he could deliver something better than what was presently on the market.

“I met my former partner in business school, and she had worked at the largest translation company at the time, Berlitz,” Shawe indicates in a new interview with Entrepreneur. “She worked there in New York, and they were constantly unable to satisfy clients. We theorized that there was a better mousetrap to build in the language business.”.

In 1992, Shawe and his business partner, Liz Elting, co-founded TransPerfect from his NYU dorm room. They didn’t have a large financial backer underwriting their ambitions. They financed the business themselves, leaned on credit cards and tried to find customers.

First, the founders had to persuade someone to hire them.

“We would basically cold-call till our fingers bled,” Shawe says.

In a recent development, they also faxed prospects and sent mailers containing information and brochures. As projects came in, they built a network of linguists to handle the work. Shawe’s description of the early sales strategy is simple: “Brute force clients in the door.”.

Shawe has since helped turn that operation into a business generating $1.32 billion in annual revenue. He notes that TransPerfect now has more than 10,000 employees, whose work extends from translating contracts and supporting global drug studies to developing software and helping companies implement AI.

It has been revealed that shawe indicates that about half of the tech giant’s revenue still comes from language translation services. The rest comes from technology consulting and other businesses shaped around customer needs.

It has been revealed that as TransPerfect has grown, so has Shawe’s net worth. According to the Forbes billionaires list, Shawe, 57, is currently worth $1.7 billion.

TransPerfect produced about $400,000 in revenue in its first year, Shawe says. He recalls that the manufacturer broke even that year, with little choice but to keep spending below what it brought in.

The founders reinvested in the manufacturer as it grew. There was an exception to the largely self-financed approach: In 1998, Shawe claims, they separated the technology business from the traditional translation operation and raised $4.1 million, with Deutsche Bank as the lead investor.

It has been revealed that after the internet bubble burst, he and his partner used their own money to return investors’ original capital. Shawe later bought out his partner in 2018.

Industry observers note that shawe does not credit the manufacturer’s rise entirely to persistence. TransPerfect arrived as the internet and globalization created newly introduced connections across borders. The founders worked hard, but the timing helped.

Industry observers note that however, as the tech giant expanded, landing work was not the toughest problem. Shawe says hiring and retaining people who could deliver the work became harder. The founders could not oversee every project or client relationship, so training employees became increasingly important.

Growth also taught Shawe a costly lesson about the difference between a customer’s promise and a binding commitment.

According to recent reports, early on, a client indicated that a substantial amount of business was coming. TransPerfect opened an Atlanta office, placed people on-site and made significant investments to prepare. Then the customer changed course, leaving the company financially exposed.

“It almost put us out of business,” Shawe claims.

It has been revealed that he says that situation was his most expensive mistake as a founder. The error was investing heavily in a venture without adequate contractual protection. His takeaway was not to make massive capital commitments for business that a customer has only verbally agreed to provide.

It has been revealed that transPerfect started with cold outreach. Keeping customers helped it scale. “If you want a business to grow, the most notable thing you can do is retain your customers,” Shawe states.

For TransPerfect, that meant hitting deadlines and delivering projects in the formats clients expect. Consistently performing well could turn a customer contact into an internal advocate, or someone willing to recommend the manufacturer to another team or division.

Shawe says referrals between divisions of large corporations is an vital source of business. TransPerfect prefers to obtain new customers through recommendations from within an organization, and much of its sales activity now involves expanding services for existing customers.

TransPerfect also organized around industries. Once it had enough banking work, for example, it could build a dedicated finance division staffed with people who understood that sector. It applied the same approach to law firms, life sciences and luxury brands.

In a recent development, the manufacturer’s goal is to become a trusted advisor, not simply a supplier accepting translation orders. Listening to customers opened doors. For example, legal translation clients needed help with electronic discovery, or finding and processing digital information for litigation. TransPerfect expanded into those services, and Shawe claims the e-discovery and litigation-support business is on pace to generate $160 million or more this year.

“E-discovery and litigation support is not something that we started in the dorm room, but over the years enough of our customers communicated to us that they needed better or different services in this field, and that’s what drew us into it,” Shawe claims.

He added that the business is now a “huge contributor” to the manufacturer’s annual revenue.

TransPerfect faces new advancements like AI and rapid translation features from tech giants like Apple and Google. Shawe states that TransPerfect must bring new technology to customers.

“We want to be the ones constantly disrupting our own business,” he says.

In a recent development, shawe has witnessed several waves of technology reshape translation, including neural machine translation, or AI that automatically translates text with advanced technology, and now large language models, or AI programs trained on massive amounts of text data. Shawe claims each change has created ways to accomplish more with fewer resources.

He notes that if formatting a multilingual manual once required 40 hours, and software can reduce that work to an hour or 15 minutes, TransPerfect should introduce the software, even if it loses billable hours.

“It might decrease our revenue in the short term, but it’s going to cement our client relationship and allow us to grow the business with that customer in the long term,” Shawe claims.

It has been revealed that transPerfect can go beyond translating words and help businesses use language technology effectively. Shawe says customers continue to turn to the company for additional languages and higher-risk content even as automation handles more work.

He advises young founders to “raise as little money as possible” and “show real revenues as much as you can.”.

If he were starting from scratch with limited money and no network, he claims he would focus on building relationships with customers and team members.

“These contacts that you make when you’re young, they compound like interest, and the value of those relationships also compounds,” Shawe indicates.

At age 23, Phil Shawe was pursuing an MBA at NYU when he had a business idea that made some people around him skeptical. Why spend money on business school, thousands of dollars, only to start a small translation manufacturer?

In a recent development, shawe saw an opening. Advertising agencies, law firms and big corporations needed language services. He believed he could deliver something better than what was at the moment on the market.

“I met my former partner in business school, and she had worked at the largest translation company at the time, Berlitz,” Shawe says in a fresh interview with Entrepreneur. “She worked there in New York, and they were constantly unable to satisfy clients. We theorized that there was a better mousetrap to build in the language business.”.

According to the figures shared by Coinbase, XRP's options-implied seven-day move stands at 1.94 times its own historical median seven-day move. Bitcoin follows at 1.69 times, while Ethereum records 1.56 times and Solana comes in at 1.46 times.

XRP, therefore has the highest relative reading among the four assets, suggesting options traders are pricing in a more pronounced move than the token has typically delivered over a comparable period.

In a recent development, at the time of writing, XRP was down 1.93% in the last 24 hours to $0.98 amid the continued profit-taking in the market. XRP briefly reached $1 on November 18, 2026, but fell afterwards as traders took profits. XRP is down 21.57% so far in November, but its history says more than its current price action does.

XRP’s average November gain is skewed upward by massive outlier rallies—specifically +550% in 2013 and +282% in 2024. Its median November return is about -10%, meaning it has closed lower in most cycles in history. XRP dropped roughly 23.42% in November 2019 and lost 12.18% in November 2025 (opening at around $2.51 and closing at around $2.20).

A weak November doesn’t always mean a weak December: for instance, after falling 9.1% in November 2015, XRP jumped 46.8% in December 2015.

Recent findings suggest that in the near term, XRP’s price recovery will target $1 before moving to the $1.24–$1.26 range. Alternatively, if the price falls further, it is likely to find support at $0.89.

#64684. Amazon threatens to leave NYC again, this time over delivery bill, as it rallies customers to fight it

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (924 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Geekwire ↗ Open Full Page

Amazon threatens to leave NYC again, this time over delivery bill, as it rallies customers to fight it

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (924 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:51 pm.
  • The Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to Fresh Yorkers’ doors.
  • According to recent reports, the legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518, would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:51 pm.

Amazon and New York City are fighting again.

The Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to Fresh Yorkers’ doors. It’s also asking its customers to help fight the bill.

According to recent reports, the legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518, would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city. Amazon is the main target, but FedEx and several regional couriers would also be covered.

Companies would need a license from the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, which would also investigate complaints. The bill was introduced in February.

Industry observers note that on Thursday, Amazon began showing Latest York City customers pop-up messages and a homepage banner that reads, “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The notices link to a form and a pre-written letter customers can send to their council members to oppose the bill, Bloomberg reported. Amazon pointed GeekWire to a study by consulting firm AKRF estimating the bill would raise consumer costs by $409 to $664 a year, but didn’t detail how it arrived at the per-order figure.

According to recent reports, in a blog post, Amazon said it relies on a network of small delivery businesses in the city. “If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city,” the company wrote. “That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in Fresh York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.”.

Industry observers note that amazon launched its Delivery Service Partners program in 2018, letting entrepreneurs start their own companies to deliver Amazon packages in Amazon-branded vans and uniforms. The companies hire their own drivers, while Amazon pays them to deliver and offers discounts on vehicles, fuel and insurance. The model lets Amazon expand its delivery network without directly employing drivers.

In a recent development, in a statement to GeekWire, Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel noted the bill “as written” would threaten more than 40 small delivery businesses the company works with in the city and the more than 5,000 New Yorkers they employ. More than 2,000 Amazon employees also work at its delivery facilities in the city, the company said.

“We’re hopeful this bill doesn’t pass as written,” Nantel remarked. “But so far, key City Council members seem uninterested in learning about our delivery operations.” Amazon said neither Council Member Tiffany Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, nor Mayor Zohran Mamdani has accepted its offer to visit a delivery facility. The tech giant also said customers sent about 20,000 emails to council members within six hours of the campaign’s launch Thursday morning.

The standoff echoes Amazon’s 2019 reversal on its second headquarters. That February, the company abruptly canceled prepares to build a 25,000-person “HQ2” office in Long Island City, Queens, after more than a year of competition among cities to host it. Amazon blamed “a number of state and local politicians” who opposed the project, which drew fierce criticism over roughly $3 billion in government incentives.

Amazon stuck with its prepares for Arlington, Va., and Nashville and didn’t reopen its search. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From a nationwide FAA ground stop to Microsoft and Chase outages that disrupted millions of customers, a string of recent technology failures has highlighted the need to modernize aging infrastructure while raising fresh fears about the risks of an increasingly AI-dependent world.

But for Jaclyn Rice Nelson, cofounder and CEO of Tribe AI, that tension is exactly why businesses should embrace the technology—not run from it.

“I don’t think that anxiety around AI is unwarranted. I think it’s very real,” Nelson told Fortune.

“[AI] is ours to shape,” Nelson noted. “And the only way you can shape it is if you understand it, and the only way you understand it is if you use it—and use it a lot.”.

Industry observers note that nelson, 41, has built her business around helping companies do just that. Founded in 2019, Tribe AI has grown to a $100 million annual run rate by helping organizations—from Fortune 500s like Hyatt and MetLife to multibillion-dollar private conglomerates like Koch Inc.—put AI to work.

It has been revealed that tribe said on Nov. 18 that its annualized revenue had crossed $100 million, up 3.8 times from a year earlier, as more clients moved AI projects out of the pilot stage. “The hard part is getting AI into production inside a complex business,” Nelson said in the announcement.

Nelson’s instinct to build something of her own predates the AI boom by decades.

She grew up in New York City with a single mother raising two children. After transitioning from teaching to business, her mother managed to send both kids to private school in Manhattan—a sacrifice that left a lasting impression on Nelson.

“It was someone in my life who had done really hard things, who I had seen do hard things, and who also refused to let things slip for me,” Nelson said.

That set Nelson in motion to seek her own financial independence. As a teenager, she started babysitting and grew the side hustle into what she once described as a “babysitting empire.”.

“I became this trusted, fairly scarce asset,” she stated, adding that she became the go-to babysitter for entire Latest York apartment buildings, with parents competing to book her on Saturday nights.

But beyond the money, it also taught her an early lesson in business: “Be the trusted person, be dependable.”.

Industry observers note that after graduating in 2008 with a degree in political science from the University of Michigan, Nelson then took a more traditional route to financial independence: Wall Street. She spent two years as an analyst at Citigroup, before moving to Silicon Valley to work for Google—and brought the same work ethic that had served her in banking.

“I moved to a new city where I didn’t really know anyone,” she stated. “And so I just worked banking hours at Google. I was always like the person still in the office, waving my hand to get the light sensors to go back on.”.

Her work ethic, and willingness to take on responsibilities outside her core role, led her to make a career jump to Google’s growth equity fund, CapitalG (then known as Google Capital) in 2015 as its first business-focused employee among a team of dozens of engineers. Three years later, she left to pursue an opportunity of her own, cofounding Tribe AI in 2019.

Since 2019, the company has grown to roughly 250 employees, after its team grew fivefold this year, the company stated—all while raising less than $10 million in venture funding and reaching profitability.

As Tribe continues to expand, Nelson remarked she’s looking for people who are deeply curious about AI, willing to take on difficult challenges, and humble enough to recognize how much they still have to learn.

“You have to be kind of humbled by how little you know every day and motivated by learning and getting better,” she noted.

In a recent development, one of Tribe AI’s major customers is Koch Inc., one of the world’s largest privately held companies. The business conglomerate employs about 130,000 people and generates more than $125 billion in annual revenue.

“There’s a lot of businesses that run through the smartest guy in the room telling people what to do. We are the opposite of that,” Chase Koch, executive vice president of origination and partnerships at Koch and son of Charles, told Fortune.

Koch wanted to bring its decades-old management philosophy—centered on bottom-up principles developed by chairman and co-CEO Charles Koch—into the AI era. Working with Tribe, the project went from an idea to a introduced product in just five months. The result is an AI-powered coaching tool designed to help employees put the principles into practice. Employees can describe a challenge at work and receive personalized guidance on how to approach it.

Recent findings suggest that chase Koch remarked he tried the tool himself after his boss told him he was taking on too many responsibilities. Talking through the problem with the AI helped him develop a plan to prioritize his work, delegate more effectively, and focus on his strengths.

For Nelson, the project and its speed points to a bigger opportunity for AI: making personalized coaching and development more accessible, without losing sight of the people it’s meant to help.

“The goal of this is not just to scale AI, it’s to make people better, to help them lean in on the things that they are going to be the most uniquely suited to do,” Nelson mentioned. “I believe AI is giving people these superpowers, and this is a good example of that.”.

For young professionals facing the same shift, Koch and Nelson had similar but straightforward advice: Figure out what makes you uniquely valuable, then learn how to use AI to make the most of it.

“If you understand the technology and how it works, what are the places you can use that power and strength to then change the trajectory of how it is used and the impact that it has on people and workforces and society?” Nelson said.

Industry observers note that koch echoed an emphasis on individual strengths: “Understand what your comparative advantage is. What is your gift combined with what you’re really passionate about learning and what gets you excited and gets you out of bed in the morning?”.

In a recent development, on Nov. 18, Hong Kong's Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) added the decentralized exchange Hyperliquid to its list of suspicious virtual asset trading platforms. The listing covers the web interface of the Hyperliquid trading terminal at app.hyperliquid.xyz/trade. The HYPE token dropped to around $65.50 on the evening of Nov. 18, and it recovered to $68.79 by midday Nov. 19, according to TradingView data.

According to the entry, the company claims to provide digital asset trading services on the website, and it has no address on record. Hyperliquid is not licensed by the SFC, and it is suspected of operating a virtual asset trading platform in Hong Kong or actively promoting its services to the public, the regulator mentioned.

In an accompanying warning, the SFC reminded investors that such platforms often lure customers with "incredible investment opportunities." The SFC also reminded investors that clients of unlicensed platforms have no legal protection if a platform is hacked or misappropriates their assets.

On the same day, the Hyperliquid Policy Center (HPC) sent a letter to the U.K. Financial Conduct Authority with seven recommendations on the country's new crypto rules. "Regulatory obligations belong with persons who have unilateral control over a function that is a regulated activity," the group wrote.

On Nov. 16, two days before the SFC added Hyperliquid to the list, Hong Kong Financial Secretary Paul Chan spoke at the Bloomberg Global Regulatory Forum. "Before the end of this year, we will introduce a bill to complete the regulatory perimeter," Chan noted.

Industry observers note that according to Chan, the bill will cover crypto dealers, custodians, advisers and asset managers. "Decentralisation does not mean less accountability," he said.

In April, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority licensed HSBC and Anchorpoint Financial as the first stablecoin issuers in the city, out of 36 applicants in the first round.

Redmond, Wash.-based RBC Signals has declared a $10 million strategic growth investment aimed at accelerating the firm’s expansion into government satellite data services and the commercialization of emerging space technologies.

RBC Signals supports satellite operators by arranging access to a global network of ground stations, including its own assets and antenna facilities operated by partners.

In August, for example, Blue Origin and RBC Signals unveiled a partnership to build out the ground infrastructure for Blue Origin’s Quartz communications network. RBC Signals is also a provider for the U.S. Space Force’s Joint Antenna Marketplace.

According to recent reports, the newly announced investment was led by Washington Harbour Partners, a private investment firm based in Washington, D.C. The firm ranked sixth among all defense technology investors in the Silicon Valley Defense Group’s 2026 NatSec100 Report.

“Our vision has always been to build a global, secure network of networks that makes space connectivity more accessible, flexible and reliable,” Ron Faith, RBC Signals’ president and CEO, remarked today in a news release.

“By bringing together infrastructure, partners and emerging technologies, we’re creating a dual-use platform that can evolve alongside the needs of the national defense and the commercial space industry,” Faith stated. “This investment from Washington Harbour Partners will help us accelerate that vision by expanding our government services business and bringing emerging capabilities such as higher frequency bands, optical connectivity, intersatellite links and space domain awareness to market.”.

Mina Faltas, founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners, highlighted RBC Signals’ role in addressing the growing demand for space connectivity. “We see tremendous potential in the company’s ability to deliver mission-critical capabilities, and we’re excited to support the team as they enter this next phase of growth,” Faltas said.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • So you open a blank document, type a sentence, pause for a moment, then delete it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that you have an idea for a fiction novel that you can’t stop thinking about. Maybe it’s a character, a setting or a scene you’ve played out in your head countless times. No matter what it is, you want to explore this new world.

So you open a blank document, type a sentence, pause for a moment, then delete it. Faced with an empty page, you wonder how your seed of an idea is supposed to become an entire book. How can a formless thought take shape?

Before you try to answer every question on your own, turn to your bookshelf. Learn the craft of writing from people who have done it before you. How does a writer make you care about a stranger, a made-up character, within the first few lines? What keeps you reading when little seems to happen?

Sources indicate that then there’s the ending. How does an ending feel both surprising and inevitable?

The following 10 books offer a place to explore those questions. Some explain how to build a plot or develop a character. Others help you manage doubt and pay attention. They all treat fiction as a craft you can study. They can also keep you company as you begin writing a story of your own and remind you that you are not alone in your pursuit of writing a novel.

On Writing: A Memoir of the Craft.

Author Stephen King has published over 60 novels and sold more than 350 million copies of his books globally. In this book, he combines his personal story of becoming a writer with a practical account of how he works. In the autobiographical sections, he reveals his early encounters with storytelling, his struggles before getting published for the first time and how writing fits into the rest of his life. He also explores the practical aspects of writing, including vocabulary, grammar, description, dialogue and revision. His approach is direct and conversational. The book also features a marked-up manuscript that indicates actual revisions, which can be helpful for writers thinking about the process of editing. Overall, King offers encouragement and technical advice for first-time novelists.

Bird by Bird: Some Instructions on Writing and Life.

Anne Lamott starts this book with a family story. Her brother left a report about birds until the last minute and felt overwhelmed by everything he had to do. Their father told him to take it bird by bird, inspiring the title of the book. That small instruction becomes the book’s central approach to writing. Instead of confronting the project as an impossible whole, attend to one manageable piece at a time. Lamott applies that approach to rough drafts and the emotional confusion of creative work. She offers humor and permission to produce messy drafts. Her advice is to reduce the task into bite-sized parts, accept imperfection and continue even when there is no guarantee of a future reward.

Writing Down the Bones: Freeing the Writer Within.

In this book, popular author Natalie Goldberg approaches writing as a practice strengthened through repetition. She offers short reflections and exercises that help writers get words onto the page before their inner judgment shuts them down. The exercises provide a low-pressure space for discovering memories, images and even unexpected connections. The focus is on developing an open relationship with the act of writing. Goldberg pushes writers to keep the hand moving and resist the urge to cross out thoughts immediately. These small habits help the writer notice more and censor less when creating material. If you spend more time evaluating possible sentences rather than writing them, this is the book for you. It has sold more than one million copies.

Story Genius: How to Use Brain Science to Go Beyond Outlining and Write a Riveting Novel (Before You Waste Three Years Writing 327 Pages That Go Nowhere).

Industry observers note that author Lisa Cron is a story coach, speaker and author who has previously worked as a literary agent. She asks writers to look beneath the surface events of a story. In other words, an unusual situation or dramatic accident is not enough by itself. What matters is how that event affects a particular person, given that person’s unique worldview. Her method places the protagonist’s internal struggle at the center of the novel’s development. The book moves from an initial idea to a developed blueprint, including scenes. Its aim is to connect incidents through a protagonist’s changing interiority. Read this when you know what happens in your novel but cannot explain why it matters to the main character living through it.

According to recent reports, save the Cat! Writes a Novel: The Last Book On Novel Writing You’ll Ever Need.

Jessica Brody is the bestselling author of more than 20 novels, mainly young adult fiction. This book organizes story structure around 15 major developments, extending from the opening image to the finale. It also introduces 10 story categories based on patterns of conflict and transformation, giving writers ways to understand the kind of narrative they are building. The appeal is clarity. The writer can examine the purpose of different turning points in their novel. What launches the central journey? When does the situation change? How does the ending express what the protagonist has learned? Read this if your first novel feels exciting in fragments but isn’t coming together as a whole.

Plot & Structure (Write Great Fiction).

Sources indicate that former trial lawyer James Scott Bell offers a practical guide to creating a plot and understanding how its parts fit together. He addresses the relationship between plot and structure and the differences between commercial and literary fiction. The emphasis is on usable techniques. Bell’s central framework is called LOCK, which stands for lead, objective, confrontation and knockout. These elements direct attention toward a compelling central character, a clear goal, meaningful opposition and a strong ending. Using these attributes, you can decide if a story has enough pressure and direction to sustain the reader’s interest. What is your protagonist trying to achieve? What prevents success? What would make the resolution satisfying?

Steering the Craft: A Twenty-First-Century Guide to Sailing the Sea of Story.

Author Ursula K. Le Guin turns her attention to the language by which a story reaches the reader. Her writing guide combines discussion with exercises. She walks readers through drills in storytelling, point of view and grammar. The exercises make this a book to use actively. Le Guin notes that the work of a sentence is to carry the reader to the next one. She addresses how to handle exposition, or how to incorporate information into a story instead of allowing explanation to bring it to a halt. Her approach connects elements sometimes treated separately, like language and pacing. The value of this book is helping readers hear and inspect their prose. A promising plot still needs solid sentences that keep the story moving.

This style manual was privately printed in 1918 for Cornell University students by English professor William Strunk Jr., then published more widely by Harcourt in 1920. Strunk’s former student and author E. B. White revised and expanded the volume in 1959. This book concentrates on constructing clear prose. It is short, about 100 pages, which means it is perfect to consult regularly as you write. Its usefulness lies in directing a writer’s attention toward language. A novelist might be absorbed in a character’s choices while giving too little thought to how to clearly communicate those behaviors in a sentence. Strunk and White set the stage for authors to learn the conventions of clear prose. They provide a foundation from which to make deliberate stylistic choices that enhance a reader’s experience.

The Writing Life: The Classic Essay Collection on the Creative Process.

Recent findings suggest that annie Dillard, a Pulitzer Prize-winning novelist with experience writing fiction and nonfiction, published poetry, essays, prose and literary criticism. In The Writing Life, she offers a reflection on creative writing, not a step-by-step manual. She considers the difficulty and uncertainty of the writing process. A line of words can lead a writer into unfamiliar territory, but they may not know where to go next. What first appears promising might actually be a dead end, while a seemingly incidental encounter might become the real subject. Dillard preserves a place for the parts of writing that remain difficult, even when the writer is attentive and experienced. She offers perspective on the patience and seriousness of writing.

Refuse to Be Done: How to Write and Rewrite a Novel in Three Drafts.

Sources indicate that writer and teacher Matt Bell treats revision as a central part of novel writing. His guide divides the process into three broad stages, giving each step a different purpose. The first move helps writers generate material and move through the initial draft. The second focuses on reworking the narrative through outlining, modeling and rewriting. The third step turns toward a layered polishing process. This final stage breaks revision into specific operations, deconstructing a large and potentially overwhelming task into a series of more manageable actions. This book is worth reading before writing the first page. It offers a practical guide to making a manuscript stronger.

You have an idea for a fiction novel that you can’t stop thinking about. Maybe it’s a character, a setting or a scene you’ve played out in your head countless times. No matter what it is, you want to explore this new world.

So you open a blank document, type a sentence, pause for a moment, then delete it. Faced with an empty page, you wonder how your seed of an idea is supposed to become an entire book. How can a formless thought take shape?

Before you try to answer every question on your own, turn to your bookshelf. Learn the craft of writing from people who have done it before you. How does a writer make you care about a stranger, a made-up character, within the first few lines? What keeps you reading when little seems to happen?

It has been revealed that orchard Robotics, an agtech company using artificial intelligence to help growers monitor crops and make farming decisions, has been acquired by John Deere. The deal was declared Thursday and the terms were not disclosed.

It has been revealed that the startup has developed a system of cameras mounted on tractors and other equipment that gather images as the machines traverse a farm. Orchard’s AI analyzes the images to generate data on vines, trees and crops, which is then used to track growth, yield and health.

“This acquisition connects crop-level intelligence with John Deere technology and equipment that can precisely execute the work in the field,” Tim Marquis, John Deere’s director of farm systems innovation, mentioned in a statement.

That includes helping farmers target treatments and make better-timed decisions about thinning, spraying and harvesting.

Orchard was founded by CEO Charlie Wu, a Thiel Fellow who dropped out of Cornell University to launch his business in 2022.

It has been revealed that “Over these next few years, our goal is to bring the power of Orchard’s industry-leading technology and AI Farming capabilities to every farmer out there,” Wu mentioned in a LinkedIn post. “This is only the beginning of a long and awesome journey ahead.”.

The startup is based in San Francisco and has an office in Seattle. Wu splits his time between the two cities and was a finalist for Young Entrepreneur of the Year at the 2026 GeekWire Awards.

Orchard has raised more than $25 million from investors, including a $22 million Series A round declared in September 2025. The startup has 45 employees, according to PitchBook.

According to recent reports, the Pacific Northwest is home to numerous agtech startups. That includes other companies that collect and analyze data, such as Loftus Labs and innov8.ag, as well as IUNU and Koidra, which are focused on greenhouse crops. Businesses tackling field operations include weed destroyers Carbon Robotics and Aigen; rock-removing TerraClear; and irrigation startups FarmHQ and Verdi.

Alibaba and Tencent put their faith in Chinese chips as U.S. curbs threatens to slow down their AI development

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tencent and Alibaba noted this week that domestic chips can cushion their cloud businesses from new U.S.
  • Both tech giants reported earnings after the U.S.
  • According to recent reports, chipmakers and exporters now need a license to sell advanced chips to data centers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tencent and Alibaba noted this week that domestic chips can cushion their cloud businesses from new U.S. restrictions on access to advanced AI processors, yet acknowledged that they could still slow the development of new AI models.

Both tech giants reported earnings after the U.S. Department of Commerce released an interim rule expanding export controls on Monday, making them some of the first Chinese corporate responses to the restrictions.

According to recent reports, chipmakers and exporters now need a license to sell advanced chips to data centers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil. The rule also requires a license for large data centers to offer substantial computing power to Chinese customers. Together, the measures are likely to restrict the amount of computing power available to Chinese companies like Alibaba and Tencent as they develop AI models and offer them to owners.

Tencent executives, in the firm’s earnings call, drew a distinction between the computing power needed to train upcoming models and running existing ones.

According to recent reports, “We actually don’t see an impact because our cloud business today is primarily running inference,” James Mitchell, Tencent’s chief strategy officer, told analysts on Wednesday. (Inference is the running of AI models, as opposed to training them.).

Mitchell added that Tencent had reached a stage where the inference could run on what he called a “surprisingly limited number” of domestically produced chips.

Martin Lau, Tencent’s president, agreed that the domestic supply chain should be able to cover inference, particularly for Tencent’s smaller, more efficient models.

In a recent development, still, Lau called the restrictions “unfortunate” and admitted that it would now take longer for Tencent to train the next version of its Hunyuan model. “It sets everyone back in China,” he said.

In the long run, Lau predicted that U.S. controls would “speed up” the development of China’s domestic chip industry. “We believe all Chinese players would actually have to rely on domestic supply chains and domestic chips.”.

Sources indicate that tencent reported 207.3 billion yuan ($31 billion) in revenue for the third quarter of 2026, up 8% year-on-year. Fintech and business services revenue, which includes cloud computing, rose 9.4% to reach 63.6 billion yuan ($9.5 billion).

Net profit rose 0.3% to 65.1 billion yuan ($9.8 billion). Capital expenditure rose 527% to 81.4 billion yuan ($12.2 billion).

On Thursday, on its earnings call, Alibaba noted its 2030 targets—including $100 billion in external cloud revenue and a 20% EBITDA margin—remain on track despite the fresh restrictions.

“Our own progress in developing domestic computing power is in fact already ahead of our original expectations,” Alibaba CEO Eddie Wu told analysts on the call. The company has invested heavily in its in-house chip division, T-Head, which it looks to list in Hong Kong.

Recent findings suggest that alibaba reported 271.5 billion yuan ($40.5 billion) in revenue for the third quarter of 2026, up 10% year-on-year. AI and cloud revenue rose 53% to reach 61.0 billion yuan ($9.1 billion).

It has been revealed that net profit also rose by 213% year-on-year to 64.4 billion yuan ($9.6 billion). Capital expenditure rose by 60% to reach 50.5 billion yuan ($7.5 billion).

Alibaba’s confidence in its longer-term targets came with a warning about the near term.

In a recent development, “The fresh compute export control rules will affect next year’s products and services, and there is still uncertainty as regards the supply chain,” Wu noted during the earnings call. He suggested that cloud revenue growth could slow to between 30% and 45%, then rebound to 50% or higher by 2028.

Wu said it was “too early at this stage” to know how U.S. restrictions might affect the development of its Qwen family of models, though he added that the company’s current T-Head chips “are already capable of fully supporting the training of large-scale, including ultra-large-scale, models.” Wu predicted that T-Head production would ramp up in 2027 or 2028. “Once we get there, we will actually be in a better position to control and pace the speed at which we iterate our foundation models,” he said.

Sources indicate that alibaba, however, is in the spotlight after the Nvidia scandal, which toppled CEO Jensen Huang last week. Nvidia’s sales team introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, before U.S. chip export controls took effect in 2022, the Information reported. Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing company, is suspected of funneling advanced AI chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls; Megaspeed denies the allegations.

Recent findings suggest that on Thursday, a group of Alibaba shareholders sued the organization, accusing it of concealing its ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed. The shareholders noted media reports of the ties contributed to a 14% drop in Alibaba’s share price over four days, and accused it of understating the risk that export-control violations could harm its business.

Alibaba did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Industry observers note that the Commerce Department faces increased scrutiny over whether it has done enough to keep advanced chips out of China. On Thursday, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released data showing the department had approved nearly 880,000 AI chips for Chinese companies—including 75,000 for Alibaba and 150,000 for Tencent—out of more than 3.4 million chips that Nvidia and AMD sought to export to Chinese companies.

Chinese AI developers beyond Tencent and Alibaba are preparing for the likely impact of tighter U.S. chip restrictions. The Information reported Thursday that Moonshot AI, the Beijing-based developer of the Kimi models, had scrapped a $150 million deal to access Nvidia’s Blackwell chips through an Indonesian data center.

The new controls also constrain the ability of Chinese companies to manufacture their own semiconductors using overseas foundries. New U.S. rules narrow the exemptions that chip manufacturers can use to ship advanced chips without a license. The Financial Times reports that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Firm and Samsung Electronics have suspended some chip shipments to Chinese customers.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 8:28 amNovember 20, 2026 at 8:34 am.

  • Their old employer is not the only one with this problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 8:28 amNovember 20, 2026 at 8:34 am.

StepSecurity’s co-founders spent more than two decades combined at Microsoft. This week, as their startup declared a upcoming round of funding, its researchers were also investigating a hacked Microsoft software package.

Their old employer is not the only one with this problem.

Recent findings suggest that stepSecurity, a Seattle-area cybersecurity startup, raised a $20 million Series A round led by Elephant, with participation from existing investors Runtime Ventures, Inner Loop Capital and SaaS Ventures. The tech giant has now raised $23 million, including a $3 million seed round in 2024. Axios Pro first reported the latest round.

The startup protects the systems used to build software: developers’ laptops, code repositories, package downloads and CI/CD pipelines, the automated systems that assemble and ship code.

The problem is that attackers increasingly slip malicious code into open-source software that developers download. That code can do damage as soon as it runs on a developer’s laptop or build system, stealing the passwords and keys that unlock other systems.

Recent findings suggest that “A supply chain attack used to take a skilled team,” CEO Varun Sharma wrote in a blog post announcing the funding. “Now one person can vibe code it.”.

According to recent reports, sharma spent about 15 years at Microsoft, where he led a team in Azure Security focused on making security easier for developers. CTO Ashish Kurmi spent nearly eight years at Microsoft before leading cloud security at Uber and infrastructure security at Plaid.

The two met at Microsoft and started StepSecurity in 2021, after working through the fallout from the SolarWinds and Codecov supply chain attacks at their respective employers.

A busy week: The Microsoft package, agent-framework, is the Python version of Microsoft’s open-source toolkit for building AI agents.

It has been revealed that it gets roughly 190,000 downloads a month. Two malicious versions published on Nov. 17 to PyPI, the main public repository for Python software, included code designed to steal cloud and CI/CD credentials as soon as Python started up, SecurityWeek reported. PyPI quarantined both versions, and a Microsoft maintainer said an investigation was underway.

Recent findings suggest that that’s one entry in a long list. StepSecurity’s announcement also cites the $6.3 billion Binance breach in October, which the FBI attributed to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group. Binance has noted the attack started with a compromised employee laptop.

Industry observers note that it also points to a tampered copy of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension that sat in Cursor’s extension marketplace for about 11 hours last month. Cursor remarked up to 5,000 owners may have received the malicious version.

StepSecurity says it documented 56 confirmed compromises of trusted software components between August 2025 and August 2026, and roughly one every three days from March 2026 through the August report.

How it works: StepSecurity got its start with its own tool, Harden-Runner, which is free for open-source projects. It watches automated builds on GitHub and flags anything unexpected in the processes they run, the network connections they make or the files they change.

In a recent development, more than 20,000 open-source projects use it, the company says, up from about 3,000 at the time of the seed round. Unusual behavior spotted in those public builds has helped StepSecurity catch attacks early, the company says, including the March 2025 compromise of tj-actions, a widely used add-on for GitHub’s build automation.

It has been revealed that stepSecurity’s paid products also protect developers’ laptops and check code repositories. Its Secure Registry service screens software packages before a firm’s builds download them from public sources such as npm, the main public repository for JavaScript packages. It blocks versions known to be compromised and holds brand-fresh releases for a waiting period, giving researchers time to catch malicious ones before anyone installs them.

Recent findings suggest that along with the funding, StepSecurity is making Secure Registry free for public GitHub projects that use Harden-Runner and run their builds on GitHub’s servers. The free version defaults to a two-day waiting period and supports JavaScript packages, with Python, Java, Ruby and Rust planned.

StepSecurity has plenty of competition. Socket, a San Francisco startup that screens open-source packages for malicious code, raised $60 million at a $1 billion valuation in May. Sonatype, JFrog and Endor Labs also sell tools that can block risky packages before they’re installed.

Growth spurt: StepSecurity says its annual recurring revenue grew fivefold in 2024, fivefold again in 2025 and more than fivefold so far this year. It didn’t disclose dollar figures.

Named customers include Circle, Dexcom, Kong, Mercari, Chainguard and XBOW.

Industry observers note that the company has 27 employees, up from four, including the founders, at the time of the seed round. Sharma is based in Sammamish and Kurmi in Kirkland, and the rest of the remote-first team is spread across the U.S., Canada and India.

What’s next: StepSecurity looks to extend its protections to agent sandboxes, the isolated environments where AI agents run code. Its argument is that anyone who asks an AI agent for a spreadsheet may be downloading and running open-source packages.

The organization claims it also intends to double its team over the next 12 months, mostly in security research, engineering and sales and marketing.

AI Is Fueling a Upcoming Startup Boom. Here’s How to Build a Business That Lasts.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1098 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Just as the Industrial Revolution transformed business through machines, mass production and long-distance transportation, AI may be powering a new entrepreneurial boom.
  • We’ve seen this before: Upcoming technology dramatically lowers the cost of starting and running a business.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Just as the Industrial Revolution transformed business through machines, mass production and long-distance transportation, AI may be powering a new entrepreneurial boom.

We’ve seen this before: Upcoming technology dramatically lowers the cost of starting and running a business. But where the steam engine and electricity offered only a first step, still requiring substantial capital for machinery, factories and workers, AI offers modern entrepreneurs a full staircase. Today, an aspiring founder with a good idea can access powerful capabilities with little more than a computer and a Wi-Fi connection. The challenge is knowing what you need to launch and grow a business at each stage.

According to recent reports, business creation has surged in 2026, with nearly every month setting a record for newly introduced registrations compared with the same month in previous years. Since January, 5.9 million new businesses have been formed nationwide — up 16% from the same period in 2025 and 24% from 2024.

What’s driving that growth? It’s not a single engine but a combination of forces, including the continued popularity of remote work and the appeal of being your own boss and having more financial freedom, both now more within reach because of AI.

In a recent development, if you previously dropped a business idea because it seemed too complicated or expensive, now may be the time to reconsider. AI has reached a level of capability that didn’t exist just a few years ago. It’s steadily eroding traditional startup barriers, helping founders turn even ambitious ideas into real businesses with less money, fewer employees and fewer outside resources.

Sources indicate that until recently, launching a firm often meant spending money before making money. Office space, equipment, expensive software and employees with specialized skills were requirements in most sectors, not to mention the accountants and consultants needed just to get started.

In a recent development, now, cloud infrastructure has replaced costly servers. No-code platforms make it possible to build websites and apps without extensive programming knowledge. E-commerce platforms give small companies access to national and global markets. Generative AI accelerates this trend by helping entrepreneurs research markets, analyze competitors, draft business intends, develop marketing campaigns, create content and automate tedious administrative work.

According to recent reports, start by asking yourself, “What do I need to reach customers at this stage, and how will it maximize my return on investment?” Use inexpensive tools to create a product prototype, a landing page or a basic marketing campaign. Talk to potential customers. Test your pricing and measure the response. Save major investments for ideas that show real demand.

AI gives founders a chance to rethink hiring. Entrepreneurs once had to hire employees or contractors before they were generating enough revenue to support them. Today, a solo founder with the right AI tools can handle many of those functions alone.

That doesn’t mean putting complete trust in a chatbot. AI-assisted work still requires human oversight, judgment, verification and refinement. And when you’re building a trustworthy brand from scratch, you have to consider accuracy, privacy and legal issues.

Industry observers note that use AI to draft routine marketing emails, but hire an experienced marketer when strategy matters. Organize basic finances with bookkeeping software, but consult an accountant for important tax decisions. Automate answers to repetitive customer service questions, but keep a human in the loop for complicated interactions or when customers ask for one. The goal isn’t to eliminate employees. It’s to delay fixed expenses until your business can support them.

It has been revealed that historically, founders moved to places like San Francisco or Austin because those cities offered concentrated pools of money and talent. Those hubs remain vibrant, but AI and remote technology are reducing the importance of location.

According to recent reports, A tech founder in a small town can use the same AI platforms and cloud services as someone in Silicon Valley. Remote collaboration provides access to talent anywhere, and e-commerce can reach customers far beyond a company’s hometown.

Sources indicate that with AI tools, you can explore many ideas from almost anywhere. Instead of asking, “Where does my business need to be based?” you can ask, “Where would I like to live while I grow my business?” That kind of freedom can make a real difference in your quality of life.

Sources indicate that forming a business and building a successful one are different things. Many of the companies registered this year will never become fully operational. Others will struggle to find customers or stay profitable. AI can’t fix a weak business model, create demand where none exists or eliminate the financial risks of entrepreneurship.

What AI can do is make the process easier and cheaper, and therein lies the lesson. Instead of investing heavily up front in one untested concept, make a series of small bets. Develop a minimum viable product. Test marketing messages. Experiment with prices. Ask AI to identify the assumptions in your business plan, then test them with real customers and real-world data.

With more than 5 million businesses formed since the start of 2026, the U.S. could finish the year with close to 7 million newly introduced registrations if the current pace continues. There’s evidence that AI may be contributing to that momentum. But like the steam engine, electricity, the internet and smartphones before it, AI is a tool. The real power lies with entrepreneurs who are willing to start lean, test early, automate selectively and spend strategically. With that approach, we may see a boom not only in startups with potential but, more importantly, in businesses that endure.

Just as the Industrial Revolution transformed business through machines, mass production and long-distance transportation, AI may be powering a new entrepreneurial boom.

Industry observers note that we’ve seen this before: Upcoming technology dramatically lowers the cost of starting and running a business. But where the steam engine and electricity offered only a first step, still requiring substantial capital for machinery, factories and workers, AI offers modern entrepreneurs a full staircase. Today, an aspiring founder with a good idea can access powerful capabilities with little more than a computer and a Wi-Fi connection. The challenge is knowing what you need to launch and grow a business at each stage.

Recent findings suggest that business creation has surged in 2026, with nearly every month setting a record for new registrations compared with the same month in previous years. Since January, 5.9 million new businesses have been formed nationwide — up 16% from the same period in 2025 and 24% from 2024.

Binance will delist five crypto spot trading pairs within the next 24 hours on Nov. 20, 2026, following a review.

To protect its people and to ensure a high-quality trading market, Binance conducts regular reviews of all listed spot trading pairs; it may delist certain spot trading pairs for various reasons, including low liquidity and trading volume.

Binance will delist GAS/TRY, HBAR/BNB, HIVE/TRY, KSM/TRY and ZAMA/TRY pairs on November 20, 2026 at 03:00 UTC, according to an official announcement published on November 18.

According to recent reports, four of the five affected pairs are related to the Turkish lira (TRY), while the last one is HBAR/BNB. The decision affects trading between these specific assets and does not mean the cryptocurrencies themselves are being completely delisted from Binance.

The exchange clarified that customers will still be able to trade the affected tokens through other available spot trading pairs on its platform.

Binance will terminate Spot Trading Bots services for the spot trading pairs simultaneously where applicable. Users are strongly advised to upgrade and/or cancel their Spot Trading Bots prior to the cessation of services for Spot Trading Bots to avoid any potential losses.

It has been revealed that in related news, Binance Margin will initiate a routine cleanup of Cross Margin accounts with collateral valued at less than 1 USD (or equivalent in other assets), effective from November 30, 2026 at 00:00 (UTC). The cleanup will be executed on a daily basis as an ongoing operational process.

Industry observers note that affected accounts include Cross Margin Accounts with a collateral value of less than 1 USD equivalent across all assets and no outstanding liabilities, as well as Margin Accounts with no capital activity in the past 6 months. Capital activity refers to any action that generates a capital flow.

For each eligible Small-Asset Account, the system will automatically transfer the collateral in people’ Margin Accounts to their Spot Accounts while the Margin Account functions remain normal, allowing users to transfer, borrow, or trade at any time after the cleanup.

Accounts with collateral equal to or exceeding 1 USD equivalent are not affected by this cleanup.

#64670. Latest Update: How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1901 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Geekwire ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1901 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am.
  • In a recent development, it has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do.
  • It has been revealed that now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am.

In a recent development, it has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do. This has nothing to do with the willingness of defenders to try. It has everything to do with the ancient truth that to succeed, defenders have to get it right every time but adversaries only have to get it right occasionally.

It has been revealed that now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI. Do you like that math? Does anyone?

Recent findings suggest that the disastrous enhancement that broke Teams, Outlook, SharePoint and other packages was not a direct attack by AI-wielding bad guys. Nor was the FAA outage. Nor were most of the outage events of the past few weeks, though who can say what’s up with those European Union refrigerators.

In a recent development, no. The true AI-driven mayhem has been predicated for several months now not on powerful fresh AI-honed attacks, but on an absolute deluge of bugs of relatively low severity that Microsoft and other defenders with a formal patch process aren’t built to process.

In a recent development, the question is whether traditional patch programs can adapt their processes to handle the deluge. Microsoft’s is MAPP (Microsoft Active Protections Program), to which the company has been committed for nearly two decades. If the industry-spanning events of the past few weeks are any indication, these programs can’t.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella mentioned Wednesday at the New York Times DealBook Summit that last week’s Microsoft 365 outage came from a latent bug and wasn’t directly tied to AI, but he warned that AI-driven patching could bring more instability.

He elaborated in a separate appearance on CNBC the same day, saying the flood of patches being applied to older infrastructure is making systems less stable.

AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” Nadella said, when asked by Jim Cramer about a string of recent outages at United, Schwab, Chase and other organizations.

According to recent reports, some context: MAPP turned 18 this year. The program, run by the MSRC (Microsoft Security Response Center), handles outreach to partner companies that gain early access to information on the bugs in advance of each month’s Patch Tuesday release. In-house, it coordinates the patch release process, just as the larger MSRC organization helps coordinate the handling of bug reports from external finders.

MSRC also runs point on prioritizing patches of the worst bugs through its SSIRP (Software and Services Incident Response Blueprint) program, itself dating to 2004. In its time, it was an industry leader in how companies can efficiently get their arms around bad bugs.

MAPP in its own way is similarly remarkable. It has undergone a few traumas over the years, usually when a partner breaks confidence and leaks the advance details it receives. In 2025, after attacks on SharePoint raised suspicions of a leak from the program, Microsoft stopped giving Chinese companies early access. But MAPP continues to tick along in a way that would make any program manager proud. Other companies have their own version of MAPP / MSRC, as do community efforts such as those supporting Linux.

In a recent development, full disclosure: I’m a former MSRC employee who learned about MAPP at the knee of the program’s principals. I subsequently tracked patch releases at a company partnered with MAPP at its highest (Validate) level, which means I was privy to the 14-day multi-stage run-up to each month’s release. I admire and respect the program… and I’m afraid that in the AI-finder era, it’s in big, big trouble.

Let’s look at the numbers for Microsoft.

Since January 2021, Microsoft has issued patches for an estimated 10,319 CVEs. (I use estimated numbers throughout this analysis because there are various ways of counting such things, including whether or not the patch accrues to an application such as Edge, which actually relies on the Chromium project for its fixes. Other analysts arrive at larger or smaller counts.).

Over half of those — 5,383 CVEs — are 2026 releases, 5,128 of which were addressed since April. In comparison, 2025’s full-year CVE total was 1,180.

What happened in April? As nearly as analysis can determine, the floodgates opened and finders (security researchers) started barraging the organization with reports.

The first quarter of 2026 saw 255 CVEs addressed over three months. April had 163, May 132; in June the number jumped to 209. In July it was off to the races with 575 CVEs. In October, the monthly count topped 1,400.

Industry observers note that most of these bugs aren’t coming from the usual security stalwarts. They’re coming from fresh finders, they’re coming in with multiple simultaneous finders not believed to be working together, and they’re coming in relatively weak.

Though the overall volume has skyrocketed, the number per month of bugs under active exploit in the wild — the notorious “zero-days” — hasn’t increased proportionally.

It has been revealed that moreover, average bug severity has in fact decreased. Until 2026, the average CVSS severity score for all bugs tended to hover around 7.8 (out of 10) each month. In 2026, that’s dropped to approximately 7.4 as of September — not garbage finds, but the sort of thing that doesn’t scramble the jets.

No surge in zero-days and a drop in severity — that’s good news. The problem is the volume.

Once bugs are received by Microsoft, each goes through a MAPP-helmed, multi-team process of investigation and patch development.

Industry observers note that since many products have several versions still in support, that often means that multiple teams within each product group are asked to ingest a bug report, replicate the problem, devise and test a fix, ensure the fix doesn’t trigger other problems or inadvertently point to a similar bug elsewhere in the product and ready it for mass consumption. Even AI slop has to be taken seriously, just in case.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, MAPP is the traffic cop for the entire release, working with each team to ascertain patches are ready, understand the nature of the bugs and what can be safely communicated to partners and the public, and ready the processes that make the second Tuesday of each month a festival of downloads and reboots. From where we stand right now, it’s all fairly… hand-crafted.

It has been revealed that in theory the process is automatable to some extent, though the success of that effort so far in light of recent events is debatable. But high volume also leads to other problems, such as exposing information on incomplete patching.

For instance, Microsoft has recently patched Office bugs that apply to both Windows and Mac, but patches have initially only been available for Windows versions.

Microsoft’s release-day information about such bugs — patching Windows versions while asking Apple people to monitor Microsoft communications for news of their own patch — alerts the world, including eager adversaries, that the flaw exists. Apple customers just have to hope no adversaries exploit it while their patch is pending.

More broadly, many of the steps in the current patching process involve judgment calls, not processes that scale well or that can reliably be handled by existing AI-driven systems. In Microsoft’s case, MAPP is a remarkably small team of humans and, being security folk at Microsoft, they’re not always the loudest or most popular voice in Redmond.

Add the mercurial nature of finders, who may or may not provide full details on their bugs (ask any MSRC person how often they receive a crash dump and a demand for payment) and may or may not disclose their finds publicly if they don’t feel they’re getting sufficient response.

Do not add the kind of defender staffing needed to handle a massive increase in volume — either in MAPP or in the individual product groups building the actual patches — because in the AI era, it’s likely the companies won’t add it either.

It has been revealed that the cracks are showing. Microsoft has been compelled to concern OOB (out-of-band) releases and servicing updates monthly since July, often within just a few days of the original release.

OOBs are important enough to merit release outside the usual patch cadence, often because there’s a security concern involved, but they’re tough on administrators already wading through a slew of regularly scheduled patching. With volumes high, patch testers may rush or elide certain steps, such as checking that a fix doesn’t break something deeper in the system.

Industry observers note that nadella told the DealBook audience this week that a patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week. Now, he remarked, the patch “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild. So that’s going to create instability.”.

Recent findings suggest that think of MAPP as Mariners catcher Dan Wilson in 2001: a pro handling a staff of skilled human pitchers, one pitch at a time. Now it’s 2026, and the pitchers have been swapped for a bank of mediocre pitching machines all slinging fastballs at … 2026-era Dan Wilson.

Here, again, AI can’t fix a system that requires defenders to catch every pitch. Secondary lines of defense that have worked in the past — for instance, the requirement by various regulatory programs that enterprises ascertain that patches are safe for their own systems — rely heavily on companies sending out the soundest possible patches.

In a recent development, managed service providers might at least make sure that patches are flagged to customers as available, relevant and urgent. But they’re in no position to do much more than trust that what’s shipped is safe to deploy and react when things go wrong.

Even that gets harder when a bug kneecaps the security tools they depend on. Last week’s Microsoft 365 outage affected parts of Microsoft Defender that interact with Exchange Online.

It has been revealed that it’s not just Microsoft, of course. The Linux community is seriously suffering, and both Apple and (especially) Google have struggled with patch-release quality in 2026 as evidenced by their own emergency updates and post-release device instability reports. Industry-wide, ecosystems built around reliable, transparent patch cadences and patch-development processes have never seemed more in danger of being overwhelmed.

What needs to happen? Sure, build those AI systems; the marketing people will be pleased. It’ll speed up some parts of the process. But a system capable of replicating, every time, the human judgment calls that go into the patch-release process isn’t going to magically create itself; people have to create it.

Is there some chance that the deluge will ebb — that researchers and their tools will at some point finally find all the bugs in all the world’s products?

It’s a pretty thought, and some relief may eventually come. When more and more unrelated finders turn up the same bug, it gives one hope that the set is finite. But no one knows when relief will come, and most folk in tech suspect that really, no, there is no bottom to the bug barrel. Nor, for the foreseeable future, any rest for the weary.

Agent management startup LangChain has raised a $300 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by CapitalG, with participation from investors, including Singapore’s GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP, and Sapphire Ventures, the company announced on Friday.

That’s more than double its $1.25 billion valuation when it raised $125 million about a year ago, led by IVP.

LangChain began in 2022 as a popular open source project that handled the kinds of tasks that early-stage LLMs found difficult, like searching the web, calling APIs, and interacting with databases. As the frontier AI labs delivered harnesses that now competently do those tasks, LangChain turned its focus toward managing AI agents. It has apparently found its stride in this highly competitive area with a simple message: letting businesses own their own intelligence.

Sources indicate that with its open source roots, the startup states its agent creation and management software, LangSmith, is not trying to lock people into any particular model, cloud, or ecosystem, unlike the major clouds or frontier AI labs. It also promises that LangSmith will contain agent behavior and is easy to use.

Recent findings suggest that true, there are plenty of other startups pitching similar advantages these days and also doing well (case in point is newcomer Mintive). However, LangChain has had a head start and now claims 7,000 LangSmith customers, including big-name startups like Harvey, Rippling, and Clay, and enterprises like Nvidia, Toyota, and Salesforce.

#64667. This Is the Reason Your AI Tools Actually Remember Anything

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1083 w)
